# Unit 4: Chemical Kinetics
## 4.4 The Arrhenius Equation and Reaction Mechanisms
*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 216 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (4.4 The Arrhenius Equation and Reaction Mechanisms):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 216):** Arrhenius plot (ln k vs 1/T), elementary steps, molecularity, and rate-determining step determination.
> • Curriculum Focus: Arrhenius plot (ln k vs 1/T), elementary steps, molecularity, and rate-determining step determination.
> • Acid-Base Definitions: Arrhenius: Acid yields H⁺ in water; Base yields OH⁻. Brønsted-Lowry: Acid is proton (H⁺) donor; Base is proton acceptor (forms conjugate acid-base pairs differing by one H⁺). Lewis: Acid is electron-pair acceptor; Base is electron-pair donor.
> • Autoionization of Water & pH Scale: K_w = [H_3O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C. pH = -log[H_3O⁺], pOH = -log[OH⁻], and pH + pOH = 14. Strong acids (HCl, HNO_3, H_2SO_4) dissociate 100%: [H⁺] = C_acid.
> • Weak Acids & Bases: Weak acid equilibrium: HA + H_2O ⇌ H_3O⁺ + A⁻. Acid dissociation constant: K_a = [H_3O⁺][A⁻] / [HA]. Smaller K_a means weaker acid. For conjugate pair: K_a · K_b = K_w.
> • Salt Hydrolysis: 1) Strong acid + Strong base salt (NaCl) → Neutral (pH = 7); 2) Strong acid + Weak base salt (NH_4Cl) → Acidic (pH < 7, cation hydrolyzes); 3) Weak acid + Strong base salt (CH_3COONa) → Basic (pH > 7, anion hydrolyzes).
> • Buffer Solutions: Resist pH changes upon addition of small amounts of acid or base. Composed of a weak acid and its conjugate base salt (or weak base and conjugate acid). Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pK_a + log([A⁻] / [HA]).

---

### 📄 Textbook Page 216 — Structured Curriculum Text

Factors Affecting the Rate of a Chemical Reaction

211	UNIT 4

Experiment 4.3

Effect of surface Area on Reaction Rate

Objective: To study the effect of surface area of reactants on the rate of reaction

using cube chalk and powdered chalk with dilute hydrochloric acid.

Apparatus: Direct reading balance, 100 mL conical flask, stopwatch, cotton

wool.

Chemicals: Cube chalk, powered chalk and 2M dilute HCl solution

Procedure: Repeat Experiment 4.1 but use 20 g of small cubical chalk and then

powdered chalk in place of marble chips.

Observations: In which case is the gas produced faster?

Observations and analysis:

1. Compare the rate curve, average rate and reaction rate at 2 minutes with that

of Experiment 4.1. Explain your observations.

2. Sketch a graph for the consumption of each size of chalk (cube chalk and

powdered chalk) against time on the same graph sheet.

3. Write a conclusion to the experiment.

Reactions can be classified as homogeneous (same phase) and heterogeneous (different

phases). For example, the combustion of graphite is a heterogeneous reaction because

it involves a solid with gas. In this case, the reaction occurs only at the interface

(boundary) between two phases. A homogeneous reaction occurs only in one phase.

For example:

NO (g) → ½N2(g) + ½O2 (g)

Except for substances in the gaseous state or in solution, reactions occur at the

boundary, or interface, between two phases. Hence, the rate of reaction between

two phases depends to a great extent on the surface area of contact between them.

Finely divided solids, react more rapidly than the same amount of the substance

in a large body because of the greater surface area available.

Acids and bases drive biochemical reactions and cellular homeostasis. Buffer systems absorb incoming hydronium and hydroxide ions through reversible conjugate equilibrium, stabilizing physiological pH.

- **Key Principle**: A strong acid has a very weak conjugate base; a weak acid has a relatively strong conjugate base.

- **Key Principle**: At the equivalence point of a titration, moles of acid chemically neutralize moles of base; the resulting pH depends on salt hydrolysis.

Agricultural lime (calcium carbonate / CaCO_3) applications by the Ministry of Agriculture neutralize acidic soils across the Western Ethiopian highlands (Wollega, Gojjam) to boost crop fertility.

### 5. EUEE Entrance Examination Strategy & Examiner Distractors

Factors Affecting the Rate of a Chemical Reaction

215	UNIT 4

Temperature usually has a major effect on the rate of reaction. Molecules at higher

temperatures have more thermal energy. Generally, an increase in the temperature

of a reaction mixture increases the rate of chemical reactions. This is because, as the

temperature of the reaction mixture raises, the average kinetic energy of the reacting

particles increases. So, they collide more frequently and with greater energy.

The effect of temperature on rate of reaction can be experienced in our daily life. For

example, foods cook faster at higher temperature than at lower ones. We use a burner

or a hot plate in the laboratory to increase the speed of reactions that proceed slowly at

ordinary temperatures. In many cases, the rate of a reaction in a homogeneous system

is approximately doubled by an increase in temperature of only 10 °C.

# Unit 5: Chemical Equilibrium
## 5.1 Characteristics of Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium
*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 222 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (5.1 Characteristics of Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 222):** Reversibility of reactions, forward and reverse rate equality, and constancy of macroscopic properties.
> • Curriculum Focus: Reversibility of reactions, forward and reverse rate equality, and constancy of macroscopic properties.
> • Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium: Reversible reactions reach equilibrium when forward and reverse reaction rates are exactly equal (Rate_f = Rate_r), and macroscopic reactant/product concentrations remain constant.
> • Equilibrium Constants K_c & K_p: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: K_c = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b). Pure solids and pure liquids are EXCLUDED (activity = 1). K_p = K_c(RT)^(Δn), where Δn = (c + d) - (a + b) for gaseous moles.
> • Reaction Quotient (Q): Formulated identically to K using instantaneous concentrations. If Q < K, forward reaction proceeds to right; If Q = K, system is at equilibrium; If Q > K, reverse reaction proceeds to left.
> • Le Chatelier's Principle: When an external stress (concentration, temperature, pressure) is applied to an equilibrium system, the system shifts in the direction that counteracts the stress.
> • Specific Equilibrium Shifts: 1) Adding reactant shifts RIGHT; 2) Increasing pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles; 3) Increasing temperature shifts in ENDOTHERMIC direction (ONLY temperature changes the numerical value of K); 4) Catalysts accelerate rates equally, leaving K unchanged.

---

### 📄 Textbook Page 222 — Structured Curriculum Text

Factors Affecting the Rate of a Chemical Reaction

217	UNIT 4

A catalyst is a substance that changes reaction rate by providing a different reaction

mechanism one with a lower activation energy, Ea

. An activation energy is the minimum

energy required to start a chemical reaction. Catalysts are not used up by the reactions,

rather they are recovered at the end of the reaction. Although a catalyst speeds up the

reaction, it does not alter the position of equilibrium.

Chemical catalysts can be either positive or negative. Positive catalysts increase the

rate of reaction by lowering the Ea

Example 4.4

2SO 2 (g) + O 2 (g) → 2SO 3 (g); V2 O5 (s) as catalyst.

Negative catalysts or inhibitors decrease the rate of reaction by increasing the value

of Ea

Example 4.5

OCl – (aq) + I – (aq) → OI– (aq) + Cl – (aq); OH– (aq) as inhibitor.

---

### 📖 Structured AI Concept Breakdown & Explanation

### 1. Theoretical Foundations & Governing Principles
Chemical equilibrium represents an energetic minimum and entropy maximum for a reacting mixture. Systems dynamically adapt to perturbations to restore the balance defined by the thermodynamic constant K.

**Curriculum Syllabus Alignment:** Reversibility of reactions, forward and reverse rate equality, and constancy of macroscopic properties.

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Key Principle**: Catalysts speed up the attainment of equilibrium but have ZERO effect on equilibrium concentrations or the value of K.
- **Key Principle**: In reactions where gaseous moles are equal on both sides (Δn = 0), pressure or volume changes cause NO shift in equilibrium.
- **Key Principle**: Temperature is the ONLY environmental parameter that alters the equilibrium constant K.

### 3. Core Reference Table & Visual Schema
**Visual / Experimental Schema:**
```text
Le Chatelier Pressure Shift: [2 SO_2(g) + O_2(g) (3 moles)] ⇌ [2 SO_3(g) (2 moles)]. Increasing pressure shifts RIGHT toward the 2-mole side to relieve pressure.
```

Industrial ammonia synthesis for agricultural nitrogen fertilizers in Ethiopian agro-chemical plants optimizes Haber process conditions (450°C, 200 atm, iron catalyst).

*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 223 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (5.1 Characteristics of Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium):**

> • Curriculum Focus: Reversibility of reactions, forward and reverse rate equality, and constancy of macroscopic properties.
> • Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium: Reversible reactions reach equilibrium when forward and reverse reaction rates are exactly equal (Rate_f = Rate_r), and macroscopic reactant/product concentrations remain constant.
> • Equilibrium Constants K_c & K_p: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: K_c = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b). Pure solids and pure liquids are EXCLUDED (activity = 1). K_p = K_c(RT)^(Δn), where Δn = (c + d) - (a + b) for gaseous moles.
> • Reaction Quotient (Q): Formulated identically to K using instantaneous concentrations. If Q < K, forward reaction proceeds to right; If Q = K, system is at equilibrium; If Q > K, reverse reaction proceeds to left.
> • Le Chatelier's Principle: When an external stress (concentration, temperature, pressure) is applied to an equilibrium system, the system shifts in the direction that counteracts the stress.
> • Specific Equilibrium Shifts: 1) Adding reactant shifts RIGHT; 2) Increasing pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles; 3) Increasing temperature shifts in ENDOTHERMIC direction (ONLY temperature changes the numerical value of K); 4) Catalysts accelerate rates equally, leaving K unchanged.

biochemical catalysts called enzymes.

collisions.

increases both the frequency of collisions and the number of molecules possessing

enough energy to undergo effective collision.

~ Reaction rate is expressed as the change in concentration of a reactant or product,

per unit time.

~ Reaction rates must be determined experimentally, often by gathering data on

the variation of concentration over time.

~ Reaction rates are influenced by the concentrations of reactants, temperature,

catalysts and the degree of contact between reactants (surface area).

# Unit 5: Chemical Equilibrium
## 5.1 Characteristics of Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium
*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 224 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (5.1 Characteristics of Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 222):** Reversibility of reactions, forward and reverse rate equality, and constancy of macroscopic properties.
> • Curriculum Focus: Reversibility of reactions, forward and reverse rate equality, and constancy of macroscopic properties.
> • Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium: Reversible reactions reach equilibrium when forward and reverse reaction rates are exactly equal (Rate_f = Rate_r), and macroscopic reactant/product concentrations remain constant.
> • Equilibrium Constants K_c & K_p: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: K_c = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b). Pure solids and pure liquids are EXCLUDED (activity = 1). K_p = K_c(RT)^(Δn), where Δn = (c + d) - (a + b) for gaseous moles.
> • Reaction Quotient (Q): Formulated identically to K using instantaneous concentrations. If Q < K, forward reaction proceeds to right; If Q = K, system is at equilibrium; If Q > K, reverse reaction proceeds to left.
> • Le Chatelier's Principle: When an external stress (concentration, temperature, pressure) is applied to an equilibrium system, the system shifts in the direction that counteracts the stress.
> • Specific Equilibrium Shifts: 1) Adding reactant shifts RIGHT; 2) Increasing pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles; 3) Increasing temperature shifts in ENDOTHERMIC direction (ONLY temperature changes the numerical value of K); 4) Catalysts accelerate rates equally, leaving K unchanged.

# Unit 5: Chemical Equilibrium
## 5.1 Characteristics of Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium
*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 226 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (5.1 Characteristics of Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 222):** Reversibility of reactions, forward and reverse rate equality, and constancy of macroscopic properties.
> • Curriculum Focus: Reversibility of reactions, forward and reverse rate equality, and constancy of macroscopic properties.
> • Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium: Reversible reactions reach equilibrium when forward and reverse reaction rates are exactly equal (Rate_f = Rate_r), and macroscopic reactant/product concentrations remain constant.
> • Equilibrium Constants K_c & K_p: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: K_c = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b). Pure solids and pure liquids are EXCLUDED (activity = 1). K_p = K_c(RT)^(Δn), where Δn = (c + d) - (a + b) for gaseous moles.
> • Reaction Quotient (Q): Formulated identically to K using instantaneous concentrations. If Q < K, forward reaction proceeds to right; If Q = K, system is at equilibrium; If Q > K, reverse reaction proceeds to left.
> • Le Chatelier's Principle: When an external stress (concentration, temperature, pressure) is applied to an equilibrium system, the system shifts in the direction that counteracts the stress.
> • Specific Equilibrium Shifts: 1) Adding reactant shifts RIGHT; 2) Increasing pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles; 3) Increasing temperature shifts in ENDOTHERMIC direction (ONLY temperature changes the numerical value of K); 4) Catalysts accelerate rates equally, leaving K unchanged.

Many chemical reactions proceed to completion. In such types of reactions, the

reactants, are converted to the products and the amount of reactants left after the

reaction is very small. Such reactions are called irreversible reactions or one-way

reactions. When the equation for an irreversible reaction is written, a single arrow

C(s) + O 2(g) → CO 2 (g)

reversible reactions or two-way reactions. These reactions usually proceed both in

the forward and reverse reactions. The reaction in which the original reactants form

products is the forward reaction and the reaction in which the products are converted

to the original reactant is the reverse (backward) reaction. When the equation for a

reversible reaction is written, a double arrow (⇌) indicates the reaction that goes from

reactants to products to the right and from the products to the reactants to the left.

Reversible reactions have the following general form:

aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD

Where A and B are reactants, C and D are products and a, b, c, and d are balancing

coefficients. In this reaction:

aA + bB → cC + dD Forward reaction

cC + dD → aA + bB Reverse reaction

For example, the formation of ammonia is a reversible reaction:

N2 (g) + 3H2 (g) ⇌ 2NH3 (g)

# Unit 5: Chemical Equilibrium
## 5.2 Equilibrium Constant Expressions (Kc and Kp)
*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 231 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (5.2 Equilibrium Constant Expressions (Kc and Kp)):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 228):** Law of mass action, relationship between Kc and Kp (Kp = Kc(RT)^dn), and heterogeneous equilibria expressions.
> • Curriculum Focus: Law of mass action, relationship between Kc and Kp (Kp = Kc(RT)^dn), and heterogeneous equilibria expressions.
> • Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium: Reversible reactions reach equilibrium when forward and reverse reaction rates are exactly equal (Rate_f = Rate_r), and macroscopic reactant/product concentrations remain constant.
> • Equilibrium Constants K_c & K_p: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: K_c = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b). Pure solids and pure liquids are EXCLUDED (activity = 1). K_p = K_c(RT)^(Δn), where Δn = (c + d) - (a + b) for gaseous moles.
> • Reaction Quotient (Q): Formulated identically to K using instantaneous concentrations. If Q < K, forward reaction proceeds to right; If Q = K, system is at equilibrium; If Q > K, reverse reaction proceeds to left.
> • Le Chatelier's Principle: When an external stress (concentration, temperature, pressure) is applied to an equilibrium system, the system shifts in the direction that counteracts the stress.
> • Specific Equilibrium Shifts: 1) Adding reactant shifts RIGHT; 2) Increasing pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles; 3) Increasing temperature shifts in ENDOTHERMIC direction (ONLY temperature changes the numerical value of K); 4) Catalysts accelerate rates equally, leaving K unchanged.

---

Discuss the following idea in pairs and present your findings to the whole class.

Why do chemical reactions reach an equilibrium state?

For a reversible reaction, the rate with which the reactants form products is the forward

reaction rate (rf ) and the rate with which the products combine to produce the original

reactants is called the reverse reaction rate (rr ). At the beginning of the reaction,

the forward reaction has a high rate, but gradually decreases with time. The reverse

reaction has a very small rate at the beginning, but gradually increases (as the products

concentration increase) until equilibrium is established. The equilibrium is attained

when the rate of the two opposing reactions become equal. That is at equilibrium:

Rate of forward reaction (rf ) = Rate of reverse reaction (rr )

```

Chemical equilibria are dynamic equilibria, i. e., reactants and products are

interconverted continually, even though the overall composition of the reaction mixture

does not change. Once the equilibrium is established, a change in one direction is

balanced by changes in the other direction.

the rate of forward reaction also decreases. However, due to the increase in the

concentration of products, the rate of the reverse reaction increases. As the reaction

further progresses a point will be reached when the rate of forward reaction becomes

equal to the rate of reverse reaction. When this stage is attained, the concentrations of

reactants and products do not change. The reaction has reached chemical equilibrium.

b. Why does the brown colour become constant, eventually?

c. What will happen to the colour, if you check after a month?

Chemical equilibria are dynamic equilibria, i. e., reactants and products are

interconverted continually, even though the overall composition of the reaction mixture

does not change. Once the equilibrium is established, a change in one direction is

balanced by changes in the other direction.

To understand the concept, consider Figure 5.1, which shows the change in the

reaction rate with time for the forward and reverse reactions. The rate of the forward

reaction depends upon the concentration of reactants, whereas the rate of the reverse

reaction depends upon the concentration of the products. Initially, only the reactants

are present, therefore, the rate of the forward reaction is fast. The reaction in the

reverse direction does not take place as no product is present yet.

As the reaction progresses, the concentration of the reactants decreases and hence,

the rate of forward reaction also decreases. However, due to the increase in the

concentration of products, the rate of the reverse reaction increases. As the reaction

further progresses a point will be reached when the rate of forward reaction becomes

equal to the rate of reverse reaction. When this stage is attained, the concentrations of

reactants and products do not change. The reaction has reached chemical equilibrium.

# Unit 5: Chemical Equilibrium
## 5.2 Equilibrium Constant Expressions (Kc and Kp)
*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 233 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (5.2 Equilibrium Constant Expressions (Kc and Kp)):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 228):** Law of mass action, relationship between Kc and Kp (Kp = Kc(RT)^dn), and heterogeneous equilibria expressions.
> • Curriculum Focus: Law of mass action, relationship between Kc and Kp (Kp = Kc(RT)^dn), and heterogeneous equilibria expressions.
> • Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium: Reversible reactions reach equilibrium when forward and reverse reaction rates are exactly equal (Rate_f = Rate_r), and macroscopic reactant/product concentrations remain constant.
> • Equilibrium Constants K_c & K_p: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: K_c = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b). Pure solids and pure liquids are EXCLUDED (activity = 1). K_p = K_c(RT)^(Δn), where Δn = (c + d) - (a + b) for gaseous moles.
> • Reaction Quotient (Q): Formulated identically to K using instantaneous concentrations. If Q < K, forward reaction proceeds to right; If Q = K, system is at equilibrium; If Q > K, reverse reaction proceeds to left.
> • Le Chatelier's Principle: When an external stress (concentration, temperature, pressure) is applied to an equilibrium system, the system shifts in the direction that counteracts the stress.
> • Specific Equilibrium Shifts: 1) Adding reactant shifts RIGHT; 2) Increasing pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles; 3) Increasing temperature shifts in ENDOTHERMIC direction (ONLY temperature changes the numerical value of K); 4) Catalysts accelerate rates equally, leaving K unchanged.

---

CHEMISTRY GRADE 11

For example, synthesis of ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen is a reversible process.

At the beginning of the reaction, only nitrogen and hydrogen are present. They combine to

form ammonia at a large rate. As the reaction progresses, the concentrations of nitrogen

and hydrogen decrease so the rate of formation of ammonia decreases. As more and

more ammonia molecules are formed, some of the molecules start decomposing to

give back nitrogen and hydrogen molecules. As the reaction progresses, the number

of ammonia molecules increases, the rate of decomposition of ammonia also increases.

As the reaction proceeds, the rate of formation of ammonia decreases while the rate of

decomposition ammonia increases. At a given point the two rates become equal, and

equilibrium is reached.

equilibrium, only the rate of forward and reverse reactions are equal. Generally, a

reaction at equilibrium has the following characteristics:

• The reaction is reversible in nature.

• There is no net change in the concentrations of the reactants and products

of the reaction.

• The rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal.

• The reaction should take place in a closed vessel to react at equilibrium.

• The equilibrium is dynamic in nature.

• The concentrations of reactants and products are generally not equal.

# Unit 5: Chemical Equilibrium
## 5.2 Equilibrium Constant Expressions (Kc and Kp)
*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 234 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

> • Curriculum Focus: Law of mass action, relationship between Kc and Kp (Kp = Kc(RT)^dn), and heterogeneous equilibria expressions.
> • Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium: Reversible reactions reach equilibrium when forward and reverse reaction rates are exactly equal (Rate_f = Rate_r), and macroscopic reactant/product concentrations remain constant.
> • Equilibrium Constants K_c & K_p: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: K_c = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b). Pure solids and pure liquids are EXCLUDED (activity = 1). K_p = K_c(RT)^(Δn), where Δn = (c + d) - (a + b) for gaseous moles.
> • Reaction Quotient (Q): Formulated identically to K using instantaneous concentrations. If Q < K, forward reaction proceeds to right; If Q = K, system is at equilibrium; If Q > K, reverse reaction proceeds to left.
> • Le Chatelier's Principle: When an external stress (concentration, temperature, pressure) is applied to an equilibrium system, the system shifts in the direction that counteracts the stress.
> • Specific Equilibrium Shifts: 1) Adding reactant shifts RIGHT; 2) Increasing pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles; 3) Increasing temperature shifts in ENDOTHERMIC direction (ONLY temperature changes the numerical value of K); 4) Catalysts accelerate rates equally, leaving K unchanged.

# Unit 5: Chemical Equilibrium
## 5.2 Equilibrium Constant Expressions (Kc and Kp)
*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 236 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (5.2 Equilibrium Constant Expressions (Kc and Kp)):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 228):** Law of mass action, relationship between Kc and Kp (Kp = Kc(RT)^dn), and heterogeneous equilibria expressions.
> • Curriculum Focus: Law of mass action, relationship between Kc and Kp (Kp = Kc(RT)^dn), and heterogeneous equilibria expressions.
> • Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium: Reversible reactions reach equilibrium when forward and reverse reaction rates are exactly equal (Rate_f = Rate_r), and macroscopic reactant/product concentrations remain constant.
> • Equilibrium Constants K_c & K_p: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: K_c = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b). Pure solids and pure liquids are EXCLUDED (activity = 1). K_p = K_c(RT)^(Δn), where Δn = (c + d) - (a + b) for gaseous moles.
> • Reaction Quotient (Q): Formulated identically to K using instantaneous concentrations. If Q < K, forward reaction proceeds to right; If Q = K, system is at equilibrium; If Q > K, reverse reaction proceeds to left.
> • Le Chatelier's Principle: When an external stress (concentration, temperature, pressure) is applied to an equilibrium system, the system shifts in the direction that counteracts the stress.
> • Specific Equilibrium Shifts: 1) Adding reactant shifts RIGHT; 2) Increasing pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles; 3) Increasing temperature shifts in ENDOTHERMIC direction (ONLY temperature changes the numerical value of K); 4) Catalysts accelerate rates equally, leaving K unchanged.

# Unit 5: Chemical Equilibrium
## 5.2 Equilibrium Constant Expressions (Kc and Kp)
*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 237 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (5.2 Equilibrium Constant Expressions (Kc and Kp)):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 228):** Law of mass action, relationship between Kc and Kp (Kp = Kc(RT)^dn), and heterogeneous equilibria expressions.
> • Curriculum Focus: Law of mass action, relationship between Kc and Kp (Kp = Kc(RT)^dn), and heterogeneous equilibria expressions.
> • Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium: Reversible reactions reach equilibrium when forward and reverse reaction rates are exactly equal (Rate_f = Rate_r), and macroscopic reactant/product concentrations remain constant.
> • Equilibrium Constants K_c & K_p: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: K_c = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b). Pure solids and pure liquids are EXCLUDED (activity = 1). K_p = K_c(RT)^(Δn), where Δn = (c + d) - (a + b) for gaseous moles.
> • Reaction Quotient (Q): Formulated identically to K using instantaneous concentrations. If Q < K, forward reaction proceeds to right; If Q = K, system is at equilibrium; If Q > K, reverse reaction proceeds to left.
> • Le Chatelier's Principle: When an external stress (concentration, temperature, pressure) is applied to an equilibrium system, the system shifts in the direction that counteracts the stress.
> • Specific Equilibrium Shifts: 1) Adding reactant shifts RIGHT; 2) Increasing pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles; 3) Increasing temperature shifts in ENDOTHERMIC direction (ONLY temperature changes the numerical value of K); 4) Catalysts accelerate rates equally, leaving K unchanged.

# Unit 5: Chemical Equilibrium
## 5.3 Applications of Equilibrium Constants
*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 239 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (5.3 Applications of Equilibrium Constants):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 239):** Reaction quotient (Qc) comparisons, predicting reaction direction, and equilibrium concentration ICE tables.
> • Curriculum Focus: Reaction quotient (Qc) comparisons, predicting reaction direction, and equilibrium concentration ICE tables.
> • Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium: Reversible reactions reach equilibrium when forward and reverse reaction rates are exactly equal (Rate_f = Rate_r), and macroscopic reactant/product concentrations remain constant.
> • Equilibrium Constants K_c & K_p: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: K_c = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b). Pure solids and pure liquids are EXCLUDED (activity = 1). K_p = K_c(RT)^(Δn), where Δn = (c + d) - (a + b) for gaseous moles.
> • Reaction Quotient (Q): Formulated identically to K using instantaneous concentrations. If Q < K, forward reaction proceeds to right; If Q = K, system is at equilibrium; If Q > K, reverse reaction proceeds to left.
> • Le Chatelier's Principle: When an external stress (concentration, temperature, pressure) is applied to an equilibrium system, the system shifts in the direction that counteracts the stress.
> • Specific Equilibrium Shifts: 1) Adding reactant shifts RIGHT; 2) Increasing pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles; 3) Increasing temperature shifts in ENDOTHERMIC direction (ONLY temperature changes the numerical value of K); 4) Catalysts accelerate rates equally, leaving K unchanged.

In heterogeneous reactions, the reactants and products are present in more than

one physical state. For example, thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate is an

example of heterogeneous reaction. See these examples:

NH 4 Cl (s) ⇌ NH3 (g) + HCl (g)

do not include the concentration of pure solids or pure liquids in the expression. This

is because, the position of equilibrium does not depend on the amounts of pure solids

or pure liquids present. The molar concentrations of pure solids liquids are constant at

a given temperature.

> • Specific Equilibrium Shifts: 1) Adding reactant shifts RIGHT; 2) Increasing pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles; 3) Increasing temperature shifts in ENDOTHERMIC direction (ONLY temperature changes the numerical value of K); 4) Catalysts accelerate rates equally, leaving K unchanged.

# Unit 5: Chemical Equilibrium
## 5.4 Le Chatelier Principle and Equilibrium Shifts
*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 245 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (5.4 Le Chatelier Principle and Equilibrium Shifts):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 245):** Effects of changing concentration, pressure, volume, temperature, and inert gas additions on equilibrium.
> • Curriculum Focus: Effects of changing concentration, pressure, volume, temperature, and inert gas additions on equilibrium.
> • Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium: Reversible reactions reach equilibrium when forward and reverse reaction rates are exactly equal (Rate_f = Rate_r), and macroscopic reactant/product concentrations remain constant.
> • Equilibrium Constants K_c & K_p: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: K_c = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b). Pure solids and pure liquids are EXCLUDED (activity = 1). K_p = K_c(RT)^(Δn), where Δn = (c + d) - (a + b) for gaseous moles.
> • Reaction Quotient (Q): Formulated identically to K using instantaneous concentrations. If Q < K, forward reaction proceeds to right; If Q = K, system is at equilibrium; If Q > K, reverse reaction proceeds to left.
> • Le Chatelier's Principle: When an external stress (concentration, temperature, pressure) is applied to an equilibrium system, the system shifts in the direction that counteracts the stress.
> • Specific Equilibrium Shifts: 1) Adding reactant shifts RIGHT; 2) Increasing pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles; 3) Increasing temperature shifts in ENDOTHERMIC direction (ONLY temperature changes the numerical value of K); 4) Catalysts accelerate rates equally, leaving K unchanged.

---

### 📄 Textbook Page 245 — Structured Curriculum Text

CHEMISTRY GRADE 11

240 UNIT 5

### ✍️ Exercise 5.7

C (s) + CO 2 (g) ⇌ 2CO (g) K C1 = 1.4 × 1012

CO (g) + Cl 2 (g) ⇌ COCl 2 (g) K C2 = 5.5 × 101

Write the equilibrium constant expression Kc and calculate the

equilibrium constant at 1123 K for the following reaction.

C (s) + CO 2 (g) + 2 Cl 2 (g) ⇌2COCl 2 (g)

2. For the reaction:

H2 (g) + Br 2 (g) ⇌ 2HBr (g)

Kp = 7.1 × 104 at 700 K.

What is the value of Kp for the following reactions at the same

temperature?

a. 2HBr (g) ⇌ H2 (g) + Br2 (g)

b. ½H2 (g) + ½ Br2 (g) ⇌ HBr (g)

3. Calculate a value for the equilibrium constant for the reaction:

O 2 (g) + O (g) ⇌ O 3 (g) from the following information

NO 2 (g)⇌NO (g) + O (g) KC = 6.8 × 10 -49

O 3 (g) + NO (g) ⇌NO 2 (g) + O 2 (g) KC = 5.8 × 10 -34

Useful information can be obtained from the value of equilibrium constant of a given

reaction at a particular temperature. The equilibrium constant of a reaction enables us to:

• predict the composition of an equilibrium mixture (or predict extent of reaction);

• predict the direction of the reaction

• calculate the equilibrium concentrations of reactants and products from initial

concentrations.

K C or K P value is used predict the extent of the reactions at equilibrium. Very large

values of KC or KP indicate that at equilibrium the reaction system consists of mainly

products and the equilibrium lies to the right, i. e., the reaction goes near to completion.

An equilibrium mixture contains about as much product as can be formed from the

given initial amounts of reactants.

# Unit 5: Chemical Equilibrium
## 5.4 Le Chatelier Principle and Equilibrium Shifts
*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 246 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (5.4 Le Chatelier Principle and Equilibrium Shifts):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 245):** Effects of changing concentration, pressure, volume, temperature, and inert gas additions on equilibrium.
> • Curriculum Focus: Effects of changing concentration, pressure, volume, temperature, and inert gas additions on equilibrium.
> • Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium: Reversible reactions reach equilibrium when forward and reverse reaction rates are exactly equal (Rate_f = Rate_r), and macroscopic reactant/product concentrations remain constant.
> • Equilibrium Constants K_c & K_p: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: K_c = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b). Pure solids and pure liquids are EXCLUDED (activity = 1). K_p = K_c(RT)^(Δn), where Δn = (c + d) - (a + b) for gaseous moles.
> • Reaction Quotient (Q): Formulated identically to K using instantaneous concentrations. If Q < K, forward reaction proceeds to right; If Q = K, system is at equilibrium; If Q > K, reverse reaction proceeds to left.
> • Le Chatelier's Principle: When an external stress (concentration, temperature, pressure) is applied to an equilibrium system, the system shifts in the direction that counteracts the stress.
> • Specific Equilibrium Shifts: 1) Adding reactant shifts RIGHT; 2) Increasing pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles; 3) Increasing temperature shifts in ENDOTHERMIC direction (ONLY temperature changes the numerical value of K); 4) Catalysts accelerate rates equally, leaving K unchanged.

# Unit 5: Chemical Equilibrium
## 5.4 Le Chatelier Principle and Equilibrium Shifts
*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 248 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (5.4 Le Chatelier Principle and Equilibrium Shifts):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 245):** Effects of changing concentration, pressure, volume, temperature, and inert gas additions on equilibrium.
> • Curriculum Focus: Effects of changing concentration, pressure, volume, temperature, and inert gas additions on equilibrium.
> • Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium: Reversible reactions reach equilibrium when forward and reverse reaction rates are exactly equal (Rate_f = Rate_r), and macroscopic reactant/product concentrations remain constant.
> • Equilibrium Constants K_c & K_p: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: K_c = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b). Pure solids and pure liquids are EXCLUDED (activity = 1). K_p = K_c(RT)^(Δn), where Δn = (c + d) - (a + b) for gaseous moles.
> • Reaction Quotient (Q): Formulated identically to K using instantaneous concentrations. If Q < K, forward reaction proceeds to right; If Q = K, system is at equilibrium; If Q > K, reverse reaction proceeds to left.
> • Le Chatelier's Principle: When an external stress (concentration, temperature, pressure) is applied to an equilibrium system, the system shifts in the direction that counteracts the stress.
> • Specific Equilibrium Shifts: 1) Adding reactant shifts RIGHT; 2) Increasing pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles; 3) Increasing temperature shifts in ENDOTHERMIC direction (ONLY temperature changes the numerical value of K); 4) Catalysts accelerate rates equally, leaving K unchanged.

---

### 📄 Textbook Page 248 — Structured Curriculum Text

Chemical Equilibrium

243	UNIT 5

### ✍️ Exercise 5.9

1. At a start of a reaction, there are 0.0218, 0.0145, ad 0.0783 moles of

H 2 , I 2 and HI, respectively, in a 3.5 liter reaction vessel at 430 °C.

Decide whether or not the reaction is at equilibrium. If not, predict in

which direction the reaction will proceed. The equilibrium reaction is:

H 2 (g) + I 2 (g) ⇌ 2HI (g) K C = 54.3 at 430 °C

2. At a very high temperature, the following reaction has KC = 1.0 × 10-13

2HF (g) ⇌ H 2 (g) + F 2 (g)

At a certain time, the concentrations of HF, F 2 and H 2 were 0.4 M,

### 0.004 M and 0.001 M, respectively. Is the system at equilibrium? If not,

what must happen for the equilibrium to be reached?

3. The decomposition of NOBr is represented by the equation:

2NOBr (g) ⇌2NO (g) + Br2 (g) K C

= 0.0169

At equilibrium the concentrations of NO and Br 2 are 1.05 × 10-2 M

and 5.24 × 10 –3 M, respectively. What is the concentration of NOBr?

Once equilibrium constant is determined for a reaction, it can be used to calculate the

concentrations or partial pressures in an equilibrium mixture. To calculate equilibrium

concentrations, follow the following steps:

1. Write the balanced equation for the reaction and then the KC or K P expressions.

2. List the initial concentrations.

3. Calculate Q C or QP to determine the direction of the reaction, if initial

concentrations of the reactants and products are given.

4. Define the change in concentration needed to reach equilibrium and find the

equilibrium concentrations by using the change of the initial concentrations.

5. Substitute the equilibrium concentrations into the KC or K P expression, solve

for the unknown.

6. Check whether the calculated equilibrium concentrations give the correct

value of KC or K P

---

### 📖 Structured AI Concept Breakdown & Explanation

### 1. Theoretical Foundations & Governing Principles
Chemical equilibrium represents an energetic minimum and entropy maximum for a reacting mixture. Systems dynamically adapt to perturbations to restore the balance defined by the thermodynamic constant K.

**Curriculum Syllabus Alignment:** Effects of changing concentration, pressure, volume, temperature, and inert gas additions on equilibrium.

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Key Principle**: Catalysts speed up the attainment of equilibrium but have ZERO effect on equilibrium concentrations or the value of K.
- **Key Principle**: In reactions where gaseous moles are equal on both sides (Δn = 0), pressure or volume changes cause NO shift in equilibrium.
- **Key Principle**: Temperature is the ONLY environmental parameter that alters the equilibrium constant K.

### 3. Core Reference Table & Visual Schema
**Visual / Experimental Schema:**
```text
Le Chatelier Pressure Shift: [2 SO_2(g) + O_2(g) (3 moles)] ⇌ [2 SO_3(g) (2 moles)]. Increasing pressure shifts RIGHT toward the 2-mole side to relieve pressure.
```

| **Examination Traps** | Universal EUEE question: predicting the direction of shift when temperature or v... | Critical EUEE Target Point |

### 4. Real-World Ethiopian Application & Technological Context
Industrial ammonia synthesis for agricultural nitrogen fertilizers in Ethiopian agro-chemical plants optimizes Haber process conditions (450°C, 200 atm, iron catalyst).

### 5. EUEE Entrance Examination Strategy & Examiner Distractors
Universal EUEE question: predicting the direction of shift when temperature or volume changes for an exothermic reaction like N_2 + 3H_2 ⇌ 2NH_3 (ΔH < 0).

### 6. Comprehensive Student Takeaway
At dynamic equilibrium Rate_forward = Rate_reverse; Le Chatelier's principle predicts shifts, and only temperature changes K.

---

> Industrial ammonia synthesis for agricultural nitrogen fertilizers in Ethiopian agro-chemical plants optimizes Haber process conditions (450°C, 200 atm, iron catalyst).

> ⚡ **EUEE National Exam Strategy & Common Trap:**
> Universal EUEE question: predicting the direction of shift when temperature or volume changes for an exothermic reaction like N_2 + 3H_2 ⇌ 2NH_3 (ΔH < 0).

**Step-by-Step Solution:**

2. In reactions where gaseous moles are equal on both sides (Δn = 0), pressure or volume changes cause NO shift in equilibrium.
3. Temperature is the ONLY environmental parameter that alters the equilibrium constant K.

---

### ✍️ Self-Check EUEE Review Question
**1. Which of the following statements regarding Le Chatelier Principle and Equilibrium Shifts is strictly valid according to the Ethiopian National Curriculum?**
- **A)** At dynamic equilibrium Rate_forward = Rate_reverse; Le Chatelier's principle predicts shifts, and only temperature changes K.
- **B)** It operates independently of physical or theoretical boundary conditions.
- **C)** It yields arbitrary results regardless of initial system parameters.
- **D)** None of the above.

> ✅ **Correct Answer:** **A** — *At dynamic equilibrium Rate_forward = Rate_reverse; Le Chatelier's principle predicts shifts, and only temperature changes K.*

*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 249 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (5.4 Le Chatelier Principle and Equilibrium Shifts):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 245):** Effects of changing concentration, pressure, volume, temperature, and inert gas additions on equilibrium.
> • Curriculum Focus: Effects of changing concentration, pressure, volume, temperature, and inert gas additions on equilibrium.
> • Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium: Reversible reactions reach equilibrium when forward and reverse reaction rates are exactly equal (Rate_f = Rate_r), and macroscopic reactant/product concentrations remain constant.
> • Equilibrium Constants K_c & K_p: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: K_c = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b). Pure solids and pure liquids are EXCLUDED (activity = 1). K_p = K_c(RT)^(Δn), where Δn = (c + d) - (a + b) for gaseous moles.
> • Reaction Quotient (Q): Formulated identically to K using instantaneous concentrations. If Q < K, forward reaction proceeds to right; If Q = K, system is at equilibrium; If Q > K, reverse reaction proceeds to left.
> • Le Chatelier's Principle: When an external stress (concentration, temperature, pressure) is applied to an equilibrium system, the system shifts in the direction that counteracts the stress.
> • Specific Equilibrium Shifts: 1) Adding reactant shifts RIGHT; 2) Increasing pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles; 3) Increasing temperature shifts in ENDOTHERMIC direction (ONLY temperature changes the numerical value of K); 4) Catalysts accelerate rates equally, leaving K unchanged.

---

Chemical equilibrium represents an energetic minimum and entropy maximum for a reacting mixture. Systems dynamically adapt to perturbations to restore the balance defined by the thermodynamic constant K.

- **Key Principle**: Catalysts speed up the attainment of equilibrium but have ZERO effect on equilibrium concentrations or the value of K.
- **Key Principle**: In reactions where gaseous moles are equal on both sides (Δn = 0), pressure or volume changes cause NO shift in equilibrium.
- **Key Principle**: Temperature is the ONLY environmental parameter that alters the equilibrium constant K.

A sample of 0.25 mol N2 O 4 is allowed to dissociate and come to

O 4

2. At 400 °C, the equilibrium constant for the reaction is 64:

H2 (g) + I2 (g) ⇌2HI (g) .

A mixture of 0.250 mol H2 and 0.250 mol I2 was introduced into an empty 0.75 L

reaction vessel at 400 °C, find the equilibrium concentrations of all components.

Consider a chemical reaction that is initially at equilibrium. Often a change in

conditions will displace the reaction from equilibrium. The reaction then shifts

toward one direction or the other (left to right or right to left as the equation is

written) as it changes to a new equilibrium state. The direction of an equilibrium

reaction will shift when a change in conditions occurs is predicted by Le Chatelier's

principle.

Le Châtelier's principle states that if a change is imposed on a system at equilibrium,

∆n. ∆n = (c + d) – (a + b)

• If ∆n > 0, the total moles of products is greater than the total moles of reactants.

Lowering of pressure will favor the reaction in the forward direction.

Increasing the pressure will favor the reaction in the forward direction.

Therefore, an increase in pressure at equilibrium will favor the forward reaction.

For the dissociation of dinitrogen tetroxide:

O4 (g) ⇌2NO2 (g) ∆n = 2 – 1 = 1

The decrease in pressure at equilibrium, favors the forward reaction.

# Unit 5: Chemical Equilibrium
## 5.5 Industrial Equilibrium Processes in Ethiopia
*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 256 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (5.5 Industrial Equilibrium Processes in Ethiopia):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 253):** Haber-Bosch ammonia synthesis and Contact process for sulfuric acid: thermodynamic vs. kinetic optimization.
> • Curriculum Focus: Haber-Bosch ammonia synthesis and Contact process for sulfuric acid: thermodynamic vs. kinetic optimization.
> • Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium: Reversible reactions reach equilibrium when forward and reverse reaction rates are exactly equal (Rate_f = Rate_r), and macroscopic reactant/product concentrations remain constant.
> • Equilibrium Constants K_c & K_p: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: K_c = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b). Pure solids and pure liquids are EXCLUDED (activity = 1). K_p = K_c(RT)^(Δn), where Δn = (c + d) - (a + b) for gaseous moles.
> • Reaction Quotient (Q): Formulated identically to K using instantaneous concentrations. If Q < K, forward reaction proceeds to right; If Q = K, system is at equilibrium; If Q > K, reverse reaction proceeds to left.
> • Le Chatelier's Principle: When an external stress (concentration, temperature, pressure) is applied to an equilibrium system, the system shifts in the direction that counteracts the stress.
> • Specific Equilibrium Shifts: 1) Adding reactant shifts RIGHT; 2) Increasing pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles; 3) Increasing temperature shifts in ENDOTHERMIC direction (ONLY temperature changes the numerical value of K); 4) Catalysts accelerate rates equally, leaving K unchanged.

---

### 📄 Textbook Page 256 — Structured Curriculum Text

Chemical Equilibrium

251	UNIT 5

### 📋 Activity 5.7

Sit in pair and discuss the similarities and differences between to the following two

reactions. Share your discussion with the whole class.

1. H 2 (g) + I 2 (g) ⇌ 2 H I (g) ∆H°rxn = -9.4 kJ

2. N 2 (g) + O 2 (g) ⇌ 2NO (g) ∆H°rxn = +182.6 kJ

Temperature has a profound effect on most reactions. Reaction rates usually increase

with an increase in temperature, meaning that equilibrium is reached sooner. Many

reactions have very low rates at room temperature, but speed up at higher temperatures.

Change of temperatures also changes the equilibrium constant values of a reaction.

Consider the KC values of the methanation reaction at different temperatures:

CO(g) + 3H2 (g) ⇌ CH 4(g) + H 2

O(g) ∆H° = -206.2 kJ

KC for methanation at different temperatures

298 4.7 × 1027

800 1.38 × 10

1000 2.54 × 102

1200 3.92

Reversible reactions are endothermic in one direction and exothermic in the other.

Consider a general reaction:

A + B ⇌A + D + heat, which is an exothermic reaction.

If we consider heat as a reaction component of the aquarium system, a rise in

temperature "adds" heat to the system and a drop in temperature "removes" heat from

the system. As with a change in any other component, the system shifts to reduce the

effect of the change. Therefore, an increase in temperature at a constant pressure and

concentration favours the endothermic reaction. Whereas, a decrease in temperature

favors the exothermic reaction.

For example, formation of ammonia is an exothermic process:

N 2 (g) + 3H2 (g) ⇌2NH3 (g) + 92 kJ ∆H°rxn = -92 kJ

---

### 📖 Structured AI Concept Breakdown & Explanation

### 1. Theoretical Foundations & Governing Principles
Chemical equilibrium represents an energetic minimum and entropy maximum for a reacting mixture. Systems dynamically adapt to perturbations to restore the balance defined by the thermodynamic constant K.

**Curriculum Syllabus Alignment:** Haber-Bosch ammonia synthesis and Contact process for sulfuric acid: thermodynamic vs. kinetic optimization.

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Key Principle**: Catalysts speed up the attainment of equilibrium but have ZERO effect on equilibrium concentrations or the value of K.
- **Key Principle**: In reactions where gaseous moles are equal on both sides (Δn = 0), pressure or volume changes cause NO shift in equilibrium.
- **Key Principle**: Temperature is the ONLY environmental parameter that alters the equilibrium constant K.

### 3. Core Reference Table & Visual Schema
**Visual / Experimental Schema:**
```text
Le Chatelier Pressure Shift: [2 SO_2(g) + O_2(g) (3 moles)] ⇌ [2 SO_3(g) (2 moles)]. Increasing pressure shifts RIGHT toward the 2-mole side to relieve pressure.
```


| Parameter / Aspect | Academic Specification & Meaning | National Syllabus Standard |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Core Topic** | 5.5 Industrial Equilibrium Processes in Ethiopia | Unit 5 Framework |
| **Governing Law** | At dynamic equilibrium Rate_forward = Rate_reverse; Le Chatelier's principle pre... | Formulated per MoE Guidelines |
| **Examination Traps** | Universal EUEE question: predicting the direction of shift when temperature or v... | Critical EUEE Target Point |

### 4. Real-World Ethiopian Application & Technological Context
Industrial ammonia synthesis for agricultural nitrogen fertilizers in Ethiopian agro-chemical plants optimizes Haber process conditions (450°C, 200 atm, iron catalyst).

### 5. EUEE Entrance Examination Strategy & Examiner Distractors
Universal EUEE question: predicting the direction of shift when temperature or volume changes for an exothermic reaction like N_2 + 3H_2 ⇌ 2NH_3 (ΔH < 0).

### 6. Comprehensive Student Takeaway
At dynamic equilibrium Rate_forward = Rate_reverse; Le Chatelier's principle predicts shifts, and only temperature changes K.

> 💡 **Core Definition & Governing Principle:**
> **Industrial Equilibrium Processes in Ethiopia:** At dynamic equilibrium Rate_forward = Rate_reverse; Le Chatelier's principle predicts shifts, and only temperature changes K.

---

> 🇪🇹 **Ethiopian Real-World Application & Relevance:**
> Industrial ammonia synthesis for agricultural nitrogen fertilizers in Ethiopian agro-chemical plants optimizes Haber process conditions (450°C, 200 atm, iron catalyst).

> ⚡ **EUEE National Exam Strategy & Common Trap:**
> Universal EUEE question: predicting the direction of shift when temperature or volume changes for an exothermic reaction like N_2 + 3H_2 ⇌ 2NH_3 (ΔH < 0).

---

### 🧮 Worked Step-by-Step Curriculum Example
**Problem:** Apply the governing principles of **Industrial Equilibrium Processes in Ethiopia** to analyze and solve a standard Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry curriculum problem.

**Step-by-Step Solution:**
1. Catalysts speed up the attainment of equilibrium but have ZERO effect on equilibrium concentrations or the value of K.
2. In reactions where gaseous moles are equal on both sides (Δn = 0), pressure or volume changes cause NO shift in equilibrium.
3. Temperature is the ONLY environmental parameter that alters the equilibrium constant K.

---

### ✍️ Self-Check EUEE Review Question
**1. Which of the following statements regarding Industrial Equilibrium Processes in Ethiopia is strictly valid according to the Ethiopian National Curriculum?**
- **A)** At dynamic equilibrium Rate_forward = Rate_reverse; Le Chatelier's principle predicts shifts, and only temperature changes K.
- **B)** It operates independently of physical or theoretical boundary conditions.
- **C)** It yields arbitrary results regardless of initial system parameters.
- **D)** None of the above.

> ✅ **Correct Answer:** **A** — *At dynamic equilibrium Rate_forward = Rate_reverse; Le Chatelier's principle predicts shifts, and only temperature changes K.*

The Effect of Change in Temperature on the Equilibrium Position

Objective: Determination of the effect of changes in temperature on the position

your observations.

S 2O7:

Converting sulfur trioxide to sulfuric acid cannot be done just by adding water,

iv. Dilution of H2

S 2O7 to obtain H2SO 4

> • Hydrocarbons & Reactivity: Alkanes (C_nH_{2n+2}, saturated, undergo free-radical substitution); Alkenes (C_nH_{2n}, unsaturated C=C, undergo electrophilic addition following Markovnikov's Rule: H attaches to carbon with more hydrogens); Alkynes (C_nH_{2n-2}, triple bond).

> • Curriculum Focus: Primary, secondary, tertiary alcohols, IUPAC nomenclature, hydrogen bonding, dehydration, and ether synthesis.
> • Organic Isomerism: Structural Isomers (same molecular formula, different connectivity: chain, position, functional group). Stereoisomers: Geometric (cis-trans / E-Z across restricted C=C rotation); Optical (chiral center with 4 distinct groups, non-superimposable mirror images / enantiomers).
> • Hydrocarbons & Reactivity: Alkanes (C_nH_{2n+2}, saturated, undergo free-radical substitution); Alkenes (C_nH_{2n}, unsaturated C=C, undergo electrophilic addition following Markovnikov's Rule: H attaches to carbon with more hydrogens); Alkynes (C_nH_{2n-2}, triple bond).
> • Alcohols & Carbonyl Compounds: 1° Alcohols oxidize to Aldehydes then Carboxylic acids; 2° Alcohols oxidize to Ketones; 3° Alcohols resist oxidation. Aldehydes reduce Tollens' reagent (silver mirror test) and Fehling's solution; ketones do not.
> • Carboxylic Acids & Esters: Carboxylic acids are weak acids stabilized by carboxylate resonance. Esterification: Carboxylic Acid + Alcohol ⇌ Ester + Water (acid-catalyzed, pleasant fruity odor). Saponification: Alkaline hydrolysis of fats yields soap and glycerol.

*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 277 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

> • Curriculum Focus: Primary, secondary, tertiary alcohols, IUPAC nomenclature, hydrogen bonding, dehydration, and ether synthesis.

## 6.1 Alcohols and Ethers: Classification and Properties
*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 278 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (6.1 Alcohols and Ethers: Classification and Properties):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 265):** Primary, secondary, tertiary alcohols, IUPAC nomenclature, hydrogen bonding, dehydration, and ether synthesis.
> • Curriculum Focus: Primary, secondary, tertiary alcohols, IUPAC nomenclature, hydrogen bonding, dehydration, and ether synthesis.
> • Organic Isomerism: Structural Isomers (same molecular formula, different connectivity: chain, position, functional group). Stereoisomers: Geometric (cis-trans / E-Z across restricted C=C rotation); Optical (chiral center with 4 distinct groups, non-superimposable mirror images / enantiomers).
> • Hydrocarbons & Reactivity: Alkanes (C_nH_{2n+2}, saturated, undergo free-radical substitution); Alkenes (C_nH_{2n}, unsaturated C=C, undergo electrophilic addition following Markovnikov's Rule: H attaches to carbon with more hydrogens); Alkynes (C_nH_{2n-2}, triple bond).
> • Alcohols & Carbonyl Compounds: 1° Alcohols oxidize to Aldehydes then Carboxylic acids; 2° Alcohols oxidize to Ketones; 3° Alcohols resist oxidation. Aldehydes reduce Tollens' reagent (silver mirror test) and Fehling's solution; ketones do not.
> • Carboxylic Acids & Esters: Carboxylic acids are weak acids stabilized by carboxylate resonance. Esterification: Carboxylic Acid + Alcohol ⇌ Ester + Water (acid-catalyzed, pleasant fruity odor). Saponification: Alkaline hydrolysis of fats yields soap and glycerol.
> • Synthetic & Natural Polymers: Addition polymerization (monomers with double bonds link without byproduct: polyethylene, PVC). Condensation polymerization (monomers link with elimination of small molecule like H_2O: Nylon-6,6, Dacron polyester, proteins via peptide bonds).

---

### 📄 Textbook Page 278 — Structured Curriculum Text

273	UNIT 6

Group Assignment 6.1

Form a group of five and explain the following facts by

searching information from the internet and any other sources.

Submit your report in Word and PDF formats.

1. Dihydric and the trihydric alcohols have higher boiling

points than monohydric alcohols of similar molecular size

(mass).

2. The solubility of alcohols in water decreases with

increasing carbon number.

3. The water solubilities of dihydric and trihydric alcohols

are higher than those of monohydric alcohols of similar

molecular mass.

4. The boiling point of a branched isomer is lower than that

of its isomeric straight-chain alcohol.

### 📖 Structured AI Concept Breakdown & Explanation

### 1. Theoretical Foundations & Governing Principles
Organic chemistry encompasses carbon-based structures. Carbon's ability to catenate into chains and rings, combined with versatile functional groups, produces the vast structural diversity found in pharmaceuticals, plastics, and living systems.

**Curriculum Syllabus Alignment:** Primary, secondary, tertiary alcohols, IUPAC nomenclature, hydrogen bonding, dehydration, and ether synthesis.

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Markovnikov's rule**: Markovnikov's rule: In electrophilic addition of HX to an unsymmetrical alkene, the hydrogen atom adds to the double-bonded carbon bearing the greater number of hydrogen atoms.
- **Key Principle**: Tertiary alcohols cannot be oxidized by acidified potassium dichromate because the carbinol carbon lacks a hydrogen atom.
- **Key Principle**: Optical activity requires a chiral carbon center (asymmetric carbon bonded to four different groups).

### 3. Core Reference Table & Visual Schema
**Visual / Experimental Schema:**
```text
Oxidation Ladder: 1° Alcohol [R-CH_2OH] ──([O])──> Aldehyde [R-CHO] ──([O])──> Carboxylic Acid [R-COOH]. 2° Alcohol [R-CH(OH)-R'] ──([O])──> Ketone [R-CO-R']. 3° Alcohol ──([O])──> No Reaction.
```

### 4. Real-World Ethiopian Application & Technological Context
Traditional brewing of Ethiopian Tella and Tej produces ethanol via yeast fermentation, while national sugar factories at Wonji and Metahara distill molasses into industrial bio-ethanol fuel blends.

### 5. EUEE Entrance Examination Strategy & Examiner Distractors
EUEE questions heavily test: applying Markovnikov's rule, IUPAC systematic naming of branched alkenes/esters, Tollens' reagent test distinctions, and identifying chiral carbons.

### 6. Comprehensive Student Takeaway
Carbon chemistry is governed by functional group transformations, Markovnikov additions, and esterification/saponification equilibria.

# Unit 6: Some Important Oxygen-Containing Organic Compounds

*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 296 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

> • Acid-Base Definitions: Arrhenius: Acid yields H⁺ in water; Base yields OH⁻. Brønsted-Lowry: Acid is proton (H⁺) donor; Base is proton acceptor (forms conjugate acid-base pairs differing by one H⁺). Lewis: Acid is electron-pair acceptor; Base is electron-pair donor.
> • Autoionization of Water & pH Scale: K_w = [H_3O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C. pH = -log[H_3O⁺], pOH = -log[OH⁻], and pH + pOH = 14. Strong acids (HCl, HNO_3, H_2SO_4) dissociate 100%: [H⁺] = C_acid.
> • Weak Acids & Bases: Weak acid equilibrium: HA + H_2O ⇌ H_3O⁺ + A⁻. Acid dissociation constant: K_a = [H_3O⁺][A⁻] / [HA]. Smaller K_a means weaker acid. For conjugate pair: K_a · K_b = K_w.
> • Salt Hydrolysis: 1) Strong acid + Strong base salt (NaCl) → Neutral (pH = 7); 2) Strong acid + Weak base salt (NH_4Cl) → Acidic (pH < 7, cation hydrolyzes); 3) Weak acid + Strong base salt (CH_3COONa) → Basic (pH > 7, anion hydrolyzes).
> • Buffer Solutions: Resist pH changes upon addition of small amounts of acid or base. Composed of a weak acid and its conjugate base salt (or weak base and conjugate acid). Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pK_a + log([A⁻] / [HA]).

C O

Polarity of a carbonyl group

Because of the polarity of the carbonyl group, aldehydes and ketones are polar

compounds and interact in the liquid state by dipole–dipole interactions. As a result,

aldehydes and ketones have higher boiling points than those of non-polar compounds

with comparable molecular weight. For example, butanal and butanone both have a

molecular mass (MM) of 72. The boiling point of butanal is 76 °C and of butanone

is 80 °C, which is much higher than the boiling points of diethyl ether (MM) 74, 34

°C and pentane (MM) 72, 36 °C.

Because the carbonyl groups of aldehydes and ketones interact with water molecules

by hydrogen bonding, low-molecular-weight aldehydes and ketones are more soluble

in water than are non-polar compounds of comparable molecular weight. Table 6.2

lists the boiling points and solubilities in water of several low-molecular-weight

aldehydes and ketones.

> • Curriculum Focus: Carboxyl group resonance stabilization, inductive effects on pKa, esterification, and fatty acid classifications.
> • Acid-Base Definitions: Arrhenius: Acid yields H⁺ in water; Base yields OH⁻. Brønsted-Lowry: Acid is proton (H⁺) donor; Base is proton acceptor (forms conjugate acid-base pairs differing by one H⁺). Lewis: Acid is electron-pair acceptor; Base is electron-pair donor.
> • Autoionization of Water & pH Scale: K_w = [H_3O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C. pH = -log[H_3O⁺], pOH = -log[OH⁻], and pH + pOH = 14. Strong acids (HCl, HNO_3, H_2SO_4) dissociate 100%: [H⁺] = C_acid.
> • Weak Acids & Bases: Weak acid equilibrium: HA + H_2O ⇌ H_3O⁺ + A⁻. Acid dissociation constant: K_a = [H_3O⁺][A⁻] / [HA]. Smaller K_a means weaker acid. For conjugate pair: K_a · K_b = K_w.

> • Buffer Solutions: Resist pH changes upon addition of small amounts of acid or base. Composed of a weak acid and its conjugate base salt (or weak base and conjugate acid). Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pK_a + log([A⁻] / [HA]).

> • Autoionization of Water & pH Scale: K_w = [H_3O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C. pH = -log[H_3O⁺], pOH = -log[OH⁻], and pH + pOH = 14. Strong acids (HCl, HNO_3, H_2SO_4) dissociate 100%: [H⁺] = C_acid.

*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 306 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (6.3 Carboxylic Acids: Synthesis and Acidity):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 292):** Carboxyl group resonance stabilization, inductive effects on pKa, esterification, and fatty acid classifications.
> • Curriculum Focus: Carboxyl group resonance stabilization, inductive effects on pKa, esterification, and fatty acid classifications.
> • Acid-Base Definitions: Arrhenius: Acid yields H⁺ in water; Base yields OH⁻. Brønsted-Lowry: Acid is proton (H⁺) donor; Base is proton acceptor (forms conjugate acid-base pairs differing by one H⁺). Lewis: Acid is electron-pair acceptor; Base is electron-pair donor.
> • Autoionization of Water & pH Scale: K_w = [H_3O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C. pH = -log[H_3O⁺], pOH = -log[OH⁻], and pH + pOH = 14. Strong acids (HCl, HNO_3, H_2SO_4) dissociate 100%: [H⁺] = C_acid.
> • Weak Acids & Bases: Weak acid equilibrium: HA + H_2O ⇌ H_3O⁺ + A⁻. Acid dissociation constant: K_a = [H_3O⁺][A⁻] / [HA]. Smaller K_a means weaker acid. For conjugate pair: K_a · K_b = K_w.
> • Salt Hydrolysis: 1) Strong acid + Strong base salt (NaCl) → Neutral (pH = 7); 2) Strong acid + Weak base salt (NH_4Cl) → Acidic (pH < 7, cation hydrolyzes); 3) Weak acid + Strong base salt (CH_3COONa) → Basic (pH > 7, anion hydrolyzes).
> • Buffer Solutions: Resist pH changes upon addition of small amounts of acid or base. Composed of a weak acid and its conjugate base salt (or weak base and conjugate acid). Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pK_a + log([A⁻] / [HA]).

- **Key Principle**: A strong acid has a very weak conjugate base; a weak acid has a relatively strong conjugate base.
- **Key Principle**: Buffer capacity is maximum when [acid] = [conjugate base], which occurs when pH = pK_a.
- **Key Principle**: At the equivalence point of a titration, moles of acid chemically neutralize moles of base; the resulting pH depends on salt hydrolysis.

*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 309 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (6.3 Carboxylic Acids: Synthesis and Acidity):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 292):** Carboxyl group resonance stabilization, inductive effects on pKa, esterification, and fatty acid classifications.
> • Curriculum Focus: Carboxyl group resonance stabilization, inductive effects on pKa, esterification, and fatty acid classifications.
> • Acid-Base Definitions: Arrhenius: Acid yields H⁺ in water; Base yields OH⁻. Brønsted-Lowry: Acid is proton (H⁺) donor; Base is proton acceptor (forms conjugate acid-base pairs differing by one H⁺). Lewis: Acid is electron-pair acceptor; Base is electron-pair donor.
> • Autoionization of Water & pH Scale: K_w = [H_3O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C. pH = -log[H_3O⁺], pOH = -log[OH⁻], and pH + pOH = 14. Strong acids (HCl, HNO_3, H_2SO_4) dissociate 100%: [H⁺] = C_acid.
> • Weak Acids & Bases: Weak acid equilibrium: HA + H_2O ⇌ H_3O⁺ + A⁻. Acid dissociation constant: K_a = [H_3O⁺][A⁻] / [HA]. Smaller K_a means weaker acid. For conjugate pair: K_a · K_b = K_w.
> • Salt Hydrolysis: 1) Strong acid + Strong base salt (NaCl) → Neutral (pH = 7); 2) Strong acid + Weak base salt (NH_4Cl) → Acidic (pH < 7, cation hydrolyzes); 3) Weak acid + Strong base salt (CH_3COONa) → Basic (pH > 7, anion hydrolyzes).
> • Buffer Solutions: Resist pH changes upon addition of small amounts of acid or base. Composed of a weak acid and its conjugate base salt (or weak base and conjugate acid). Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pK_a + log([A⁻] / [HA]).

---

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Key Principle**: A strong acid has a very weak conjugate base; a weak acid has a relatively strong conjugate base.
- **Key Principle**: Buffer capacity is maximum when [acid] = [conjugate base], which occurs when pH = pK_a.
- **Key Principle**: At the equivalence point of a titration, moles of acid chemically neutralize moles of base; the resulting pH depends on salt hydrolysis.

**Visual / Experimental Schema:**
```text
Buffer Action Mechanism: Incoming H⁺ neutralized by conjugate base: [A⁻ + H⁺ → HA]. Incoming OH⁻ neutralized by weak acid: [HA + OH⁻ → A⁻ + H_2O]. pH remains virtually constant.
```

# Unit 6: Some Important Oxygen-Containing Organic Compounds
## 6.3 Carboxylic Acids: Synthesis and Acidity
*Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry Student Textbook • Textbook Page 312 of 200 • Grade 11 - Natural Science Chemistry — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (6.3 Carboxylic Acids: Synthesis and Acidity):**

> • Curriculum Focus: Carboxyl group resonance stabilization, inductive effects on pKa, esterification, and fatty acid classifications.
> • Acid-Base Definitions: Arrhenius: Acid yields H⁺ in water; Base yields OH⁻. Brønsted-Lowry: Acid is proton (H⁺) donor; Base is proton acceptor (forms conjugate acid-base pairs differing by one H⁺). Lewis: Acid is electron-pair acceptor; Base is electron-pair donor.
> • Autoionization of Water & pH Scale: K_w = [H_3O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C. pH = -log[H_3O⁺], pOH = -log[OH⁻], and pH + pOH = 14. Strong acids (HCl, HNO_3, H_2SO_4) dissociate 100%: [H⁺] = C_acid.
> • Weak Acids & Bases: Weak acid equilibrium: HA + H_2O ⇌ H_3O⁺ + A⁻. Acid dissociation constant: K_a = [H_3O⁺][A⁻] / [HA]. Smaller K_a means weaker acid. For conjugate pair: K_a · K_b = K_w.

> • Autoionization of Water & pH Scale: K_w = [H_3O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C. pH = -log[H_3O⁺], pOH = -log[OH⁻], and pH + pOH = 14. Strong acids (HCl, HNO_3, H_2SO_4) dissociate 100%: [H⁺] = C_acid.

> • Autoionization of Water & pH Scale: K_w = [H_3O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C. pH = -log[H_3O⁺], pOH = -log[OH⁻], and pH + pOH = 14. Strong acids (HCl, HNO_3, H_2SO_4) dissociate 100%: [H⁺] = C_acid.
> • Weak Acids & Bases: Weak acid equilibrium: HA + H_2O ⇌ H_3O⁺ + A⁻. Acid dissociation constant: K_a = [H_3O⁺][A⁻] / [HA]. Smaller K_a means weaker acid. For conjugate pair: K_a · K_b = K_w.

> • Curriculum Focus: Triglyceride structures, saturated vs unsaturated fatty acids, catalytic hydrogenation of oils, and lipid oxidation.
> • Acid-Base Definitions: Arrhenius: Acid yields H⁺ in water; Base yields OH⁻. Brønsted-Lowry: Acid is proton (H⁺) donor; Base is proton acceptor (forms conjugate acid-base pairs differing by one H⁺). Lewis: Acid is electron-pair acceptor; Base is electron-pair donor.
> • Autoionization of Water & pH Scale: K_w = [H_3O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C. pH = -log[H_3O⁺], pOH = -log[OH⁻], and pH + pOH = 14. Strong acids (HCl, HNO_3, H_2SO_4) dissociate 100%: [H⁺] = C_acid.
> • Weak Acids & Bases: Weak acid equilibrium: HA + H_2O ⇌ H_3O⁺ + A⁻. Acid dissociation constant: K_a = [H_3O⁺][A⁻] / [HA]. Smaller K_a means weaker acid. For conjugate pair: K_a · K_b = K_w.
> • Salt Hydrolysis: 1) Strong acid + Strong base salt (NaCl) → Neutral (pH = 7); 2) Strong acid + Weak base salt (NH_4Cl) → Acidic (pH < 7, cation hydrolyzes); 3) Weak acid + Strong base salt (CH_3COONa) → Basic (pH > 7, anion hydrolyzes).
> • Buffer Solutions: Resist pH changes upon addition of small amounts of acid or base. Composed of a weak acid and its conjugate base salt (or weak base and conjugate acid). Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pK_a + log([A⁻] / [HA]).

> • Acid-Base Definitions: Arrhenius: Acid yields H⁺ in water; Base yields OH⁻. Brønsted-Lowry: Acid is proton (H⁺) donor; Base is proton acceptor (forms conjugate acid-base pairs differing by one H⁺). Lewis: Acid is electron-pair acceptor; Base is electron-pair donor.
> • Autoionization of Water & pH Scale: K_w = [H_3O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C. pH = -log[H_3O⁺], pOH = -log[OH⁻], and pH + pOH = 14. Strong acids (HCl, HNO_3, H_2SO_4) dissociate 100%: [H⁺] = C_acid.
> • Weak Acids & Bases: Weak acid equilibrium: HA + H_2O ⇌ H_3O⁺ + A⁻. Acid dissociation constant: K_a = [H_3O⁺][A⁻] / [HA]. Smaller K_a means weaker acid. For conjugate pair: K_a · K_b = K_w.

Fats and Oils

325	UNIT 6

The various carbon atoms in fats and oils have different oxidation numbers, which

are used as indicators of their energy contents. The lower the oxidation number the

higher the energy content of the substance. In oils double bonded carbon atoms have

sp 2 hybridization, while in fats all carbon atoms in the hydrocarbon tails have sp3

hybridization.

Vegetable oils differ from animal fats in possessing a higher degree of unsaturation,

but could have double bonds. The number of fats also contain sites of unsaturation like

vegetable oils. Unsaturation in fat tends to lower its melting point and thus tends to

make it a liquid at room temperature.

Saturated fat is found in many foods including:

• Animal foods (like beef, chicken, lamb, pork, and veal)

• Coconut, palm, and palm kernel oils

• Dairy products (like butter, cheese, and whole milk) and lard.

Unsaturated fats are found in two main types: mono or polyunsaturated fats (oils):

• which can be found in avocados, nuts and seeds (like

cashews, pecans, almonds, and peanuts), vegetable oils (like canola, olive,

peanut, safflower, sesame, and sunflower).

• Polyunsaturated fat, which can be found in fatty fish (like herring, mackerel,

salmon, trout and smelt), fish oils, nuts and seeds (like cashews, pecans,

almonds and peanuts), vegetable oils (like canola, corn, flaxseed, soybean and

sunflower).

### 1. Theoretical Foundations & Governing Principles
Atomic theory reveals subatomic structure. Protons define element identity Z, neutrons dictate isotopic mass A, and extranuclear valence electrons govern chemical bonding and periodic placement.

**Curriculum Syllabus Alignment:** Atomic radii, ionic radii, ionization energy trends, electron affinity, and electronegativity scales.

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Key Principle**: Rutherford's gold foil experiment proved the atom is mostly empty space with a dense, positively charged nucleus.
- **Key Principle**: Isotopes share identical chemical properties (same electron configuration) but differ in physical mass.
- **Key Principle**: Period number equals the number of occupied electron shells; Group number dictates valence electron count.
